newsitem.title: USA: Radiation seen as new aid in angioplasty.
newsitem.headline: Radiation seen as new aid in angioplasty.

text.p: NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 11, Reuter - Briefly applying a small dose of radiation could help prevent the reclosure of blood vessels that often reverses the gains of angioplasty, researchers said on Monday.
Small mesh-like metal tubes known as stents are now widely used to hold open damaged blood vessels after angioplasty, which uses a tiny balloon to widen clogged blood vessels.

While stents help keep blood vessels from collapsing, they do not solve and can worsen the scarring and cell growth that can reclose the site widened, researchers said at the annual scientific sessions of the American Heart Association.
This cell growth can obstruct the blood vessel again in about 30 percent of people who undergo angioplasty, the heart association said.

Researchers at Scripps Clinic in La Jolla, Calif. implanted a radioactive "ribbon" inside implanted stents in patients at the site where their arteries were opened through angioplasty. The ribbons were there for about 30 minutes. The effort was to prevent reclosure of the blood vessel, known as restenosis. In the study, 26 people undergoing angioplasty and stent implantation received the radiation. Twenty-nine got angioplasty and the stent but no radiation.

After six months, 16.7 percent of the radiation-treated group had restenosis, compared with 53.6 percent who did not receive radiation, said Paul Teirstein, director of interventional cardiology at the Scripps Clinic.

After 12 months, the number of deaths, heart attacks and need for repeat angioplasty or bypass surgery was 15.4 percent in the radiation-treated group and 48.3 percent in those who did not receive radiation.
"We were able to show a dramatic reduction in restenosis," Teirstein said. To date no negative side effects of the treatment have been seen, he said.
Restenosis is usually treated by a repeat angioplasty, implantation of a stent or coronary bypass surgery.

The research could be a boost for companies working to develop the radiation treatments to prevent restinosis, including Novoste Corp, which is entering Phase II clinical trials early next year, and Isostent Inc.
